key_insight: A small number of retrieved visual examples used to augment text prompts can substantially close the gap between open‑vocabulary segmentation and fully supervised methods, by reducing semantic ambiguity and providing pixel‑level cues missing from image‑level VLM supervision.
problem_solved: Open‑vocabulary segmentation suffers from coarse image‑level supervision and ambiguous natural language prompts; the paper asks whether adding a few visual examples (few‑shot) can bridge that supervision gap and improve pixel‑level predictions for arbitrary text‑specified categories.
method: Retrieve a few class‑relevant visual exemplars via VLM embeddings to enrich each textual prompt with concrete visual context.
Use exemplar‑conditioned segmentation (integrating exemplar visuals with VLM pixel features) to produce refined masks for open‑vocabulary categories.
Systematically evaluate few‑shot trade‑offs and perform ablations to quantify how many examples are needed and where gains plateau.
impact: Makes open‑vocabulary segmentation far more practical by reducing the need for dense annotations and enabling fast domain adaptation with only a handful of examples — lowering cost and accelerating deployment for real‑world tasks.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: retrieve exemplars → augment prompt → exemplar‑conditioned segmentation (show data flow between text, exemplars, image features).
Before/after mask visual: same image segmented with vanilla VLM prompt vs. with retrieved exemplars to show qualitative improvement.
Bar/line chart: performance (mIoU) vs. number of retrieved examples to illustrate diminishing returns and the few‑shot sweet spot.
A compact table or icons summarizing benefits: fewer labels, faster adaptation, better precision/recall.
paper_title: Retrieve and Segment: Are a Few Examples Enough to Bridge the Supervision Gap in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation?
paper_authors: Tilemachos Aravanis, Vladan Stojnić, Bill Psomas, Nikos Komodakis, Giorgos Tolias
